709256.t: From Proto-Hellenic *néwos (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀚𐀺 (ne-wo)), from Proto-Indo-European *néwos. Cognates include Old English nīewe (English new), Latin novus, Sanskrit नव॑ (náva), and Avestan 𐬥𐬀𐬎𐬎𐬀 (nauua).

709247.t: Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“to perish”); further discussion of the morphology follows below.

709281.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *nebʰ- Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos Proto-Hellenic *népʰos Ancient Greek νέφος From Proto-Hellenic *népʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”).

709277.t: From Proto-Indo-European *nebʰ-el-h₂ (“cloud”). Related to νέφος (néphos, “cloud”), Latin nebula (“fog, cloud”).

709275.t: From Proto-Indo-European *snḗh₁wr̥ (“band, sinew”). Cognate with Latin nervus, English sinew, Sanskrit स्नावन् (snā́van, “tendon, muscle, sinew”), Old Armenian նեարդ (neard), and Avestan 𐬯𐬥𐬁𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬭𐬆 (snāuuar^ə).

709292.t: From νέω (néō). The dental enlargement in this term is comparable to other Greek terms such as κνήθω (knḗthō).

709282.t: From Proto-Hellenic *nekʷʰrós, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷʰrós. Cognates include Latin nefrōnes and Proto-Germanic *neurô.

709253.t: From Proto-Hellenic *némō, from Proto-Indo-European *ném-e-ti (“to assign, allot; take”). Cognate with English numb, Dutch nemen, German nehmen, and Albanian njeh (“count”), nëmë (“curse”).

709208.t: From Proto-Hellenic *nā́us, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us (“boat”), cognate with Latin nāvis, Persian ناو (nâv), and Sanskrit नौ (nau, “ship”), नाव (nāva, “ship”).

709246.t: Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neyk- (“to attack, start vehemently”), cognate with Lithuanian ap-ni̇̀kti (“to attack”), su-ni̇̀kti (“to attack”), Latvian nikns (“bad, grim, vehement”), Albanian nis, and possibly Russian в-никнуть (v-niknutʹ),…

709295.t: The word is presumably the negative prefix νη- (nē-), but the stem is unclear.

709291.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₁enos (“that one”), the source of Latin nē (“truly!”), enim (“truly”).

709232.t: From νεανίας (neanías) (ultimately from νέος (néos, “young, new”)) with the suffix -ίσκος (-ískos), diminutive in form but not necessarily in force.

709236.t: Some have tried a connection with Old Armenian ներկ (nerk, “color”), deriving both from a Proto-Indo-European root *(s)negʷro-, because often the deer and the hind are called after their variegated color (compare πρόξ (próx, “roe deer”) and περκνός…

709258.t: From νέος (néos, “young”) + -της (-tēs). Diachronically from Proto-Hellenic *newótāts, from Proto-Indo-European *néwoteh₂ts (“newness”); cognate with Latin novitās, Sanskrit नवता (návatā).

709273.t: From the same root as νεῦρον (neûron).

709257.t: Formed from νέος (néos, “new”), probably after the example of περισσός (perissós, “extraordinary, prodigious”), ἔπισσαι (épissai) or μέτασσαι (métassai).

709276.t: From Proto-Indo-European *new- (“to nod”). Cognate with Latin nutō (“to nod”), Sanskrit नव॑ते (návate).

709293.t: From νήχω (nḗkhō, “to swim”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂- (“to flow, to swim”), + -τός (-tós).
